items.title: AMD dives on short-seller report of alleged China exposure
items.summary: AMD closed down over 7% after a short-seller alleged that its firmware showed up at a blacklisted Chinese company. The company said it complies with U.S. law.
items.body: Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips." The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

items.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
items.summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
items.body: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion. The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology. Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share , showing there is plenty of excitement around AI. Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it? In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading.

items.body: Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse. Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes: This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value.

items.title: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
items.summary: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.
items.body: Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange. Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot. The stock opened at $111.50 — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI , as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months. The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion. This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion. Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT -maker OpenAI, has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

items.title: Peterson: Nvidia’s leadership crisis tests the chipmaker’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
items.summary: The tech giant's web of ties to other companies is raising the possibility that it could do far-reaching economic and financial damage.
items.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector.

items.title: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
items.summary: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.
items.body: It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice. Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world. But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away. So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer." The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic. Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

items.title: ‘Pot luck service’: Royal Mail on course to miss delivery targets for fourth year in a row
items.summary: Citizens Advice criticises company for failing to meet Ofcom requirements while reporting increased revenue Royal Mail has been accused of offering a “pot luck service” to consumers as it looks likely to miss first-class delivery targets for the fourth consecutive year. The…
items.body: Royal Mail has been accused of offering a “pot luck service” to consumers as it looks likely to miss first-class delivery targets for the fourth consecutive year. The postal service, whose parent company was bought for £3.6bn by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský last year, is meant to deliver 90% of its first-class post by the next working day and 95% of second-class post within three working days according to targets set by the regulator, Ofcom. But it delivered only 82.5% of first-class mail within target in the second quarter of this year, down from 85% in the first quarter. Second-class deliveries slipped to 87.2% arriving within three working days, compared with 91.4% in the previous quarter. On Thursday, Royal Mail said it did not expect to meet its targets until next April.

items.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure

items.body: As Donald Trump , Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support. For Iran , relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow. Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran . But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.

items.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
items.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
items.body: In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars. The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least. Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday. At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each. So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy? In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

items.title: AI demand will push up interest rates around the world, IMF head warns
items.summary: Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’ Business live – latest updates Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the…
items.body: Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned. Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world. She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe. Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen , Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

items.title: Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access
items.summary: Kash Patel missed a congressional hearing after appearing the night before at a Mar-a-Lago gala offering donors of $50,000 access to top officials.
items.body: After a string of outages disrupted airlines , banks and even the National Security Agency , U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen. The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash , a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person . Mullin appeared before lawmakers Wednesday morning at the House Homeland Security Committee's annual threat assessment hearing. Patel sent his deputy instead. And as the hearing got underway, a Justice Department jet that's been used by Patel before was still flying back from Florida.

items.summary: A former McDonald's worker calls on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees” as a judge rules a legal case against the chain can go ahead.
items.body: A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”. Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18. Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed. McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority." The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

items.title: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
items.summary: The company counts physicists, a former journalist and an associate of the pope among its guiding lights The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of…
items.body: The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations. The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price. Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

items.title: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions
items.summary: It follows months of tensions after President Donald Trump repeatedly said the U.S. should take control of Greenland for national security reasons.
items.body: Danish lawmakers on Thursday approved a security agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump covering Greenland, seeking to end months of strained diplomatic tensions over the island's future. Trump and the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September. It allows Washington to expand its military presence on the island, paving the way for two new bases and the construction of a " Golden Dome " missile defense system. Thursday's approval follows a protracted period in which Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory. Tensions reached fever pitch in January as the president repeatedly insisted that the U.S. needed Greenland for its national security, at times declining to rule out using military force to acquire it.

items.title: Viagogo may have broken law on hidden fees, watchdog provisionally finds
items.summary: The UK's competition body says initial findings suggest the ticket-reselling website used drip pricing.
items.body: Ticket-reselling site Viagogo may have broken the law on hidden fees, the UK's competition body has said in a provisional finding. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it found that Viagogo failed to show consumers the total price upfront when they were buying tickets "and added fees later in the process, a practice known as drip pricing". The CMA added that this was an initial finding, and it should not be assumed that the company had actually broken the law. In a statement, Viagogo said it was co-operating fully with the CMA, adding that the investigation was continuing and "no final findings have been made". The CMA said last year that it was investigating a number of companies over their online pricing practices, including Viagogo.

items.title: Nvidia approaches Arm boss Rene Haas in search for new CEO
items.summary: CEO of Cambridge-based firm viewed as leading contender to replace co-founder Jensen Huang according to reports Business live – latest updates Nvidia’s headhunters have reportedly approached the chief executive of the Cambridge-based chip company Arm, in its search for a new…
items.body: Nvidia’s headhunters have reportedly approached the chief executive of the Cambridge-based chip company Arm, in its search for a new leader after Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit. Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company’s board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg. It reported that Rene Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, is among those approached. Nvidia is searching for a replacement for Huang, one of the firm’s founders, who resigned last week after he admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of spying for China . Haas, 64, is viewed as the leading contender for the top job at Nvidia , having previously worked at the $3.6tn (£2.8tn) company for seven years as the general manager of its computing products.

items.title: Crew unaware of risks before Mike Lynch's yacht Bayesian sank, say investigators
items.summary: The vessel sank off the coast of northern Sicily, killing seven people including British tech tycoon Mike Lynch.
items.body: The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say. British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024. The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said. Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said. "It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves.

items.summary: Cuts – which exclude shop floor and aircraft maintenance – prompt calls for more orders to support British defence contractor BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, prompting calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s…
items.body: BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, prompting calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor. The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”. The cuts represent about 2% of its 50,000-strong workforce in the UK, which includes about 18,500 in its air business and about 1,000 in its head office in London. They will be made through voluntary redundancies and will exclude people working on the shop floor, aircraft maintenance at RAF bases and early career trainees.

items.summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.
items.body: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats. The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based. Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president. Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans. The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera . items.title: Musk says Jensen Huang is irreplaceable, regrets midterm spending
items.summary: Elon Musk spoke about Jensen Huang, his U.S. midterms spending and overlaps between SpaceX and Tesla at the Dealbook Summit.
items.body: Elon Musk compared Jensen Huang 's departure from Nvidia to kicking Michael Jordan off a team on a winning streak, while also expressing regret over how much he spent on the U.S. midterms. "You've got a winning streak ... and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team," Musk told Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Wednesday. He added, "Doesn't seem like a smart decision to me." Huang resigned last week following pressure after disclosing an affair with a woman who reportedly was suspected of being a Chinese spy, alongside reports of relationships with employees. He is expected to testify before the U.S. Congress next month around national-security and export-control issues. The SpaceX and Tesla chief executive, who previously said it would be an "honor" to hire the Nvidia co-founder, added that no one could really replace Huang.

items.title: Gilts v kilts: What is happening with Scottish government bonds?
items.summary: MSPs have heard both the pros and cons of the government's plan to launch its first ever bond to the market.
items.body: The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds. The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments. The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads. Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate. This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards. A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term. In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks.

items.title: EDF snaps up 1.3m more customers after Utilita takeover

items.body: EDF Energy will grow its share of the UK’s household energy market to more than 6m customer accounts after snapping up the pay-as-you-go supplier Utilita. Great Britain’s fourth-largest energy supplier expects to complete the takeover early next year, adding 1.3m accounts to its customer base and taking on Utilita’s 1,500 staff. The price of the deal was undisclosed. The pair will continue to serve their customers independently until the deal concludes. Utilita customers will be contacted about any changes to their service. After the deal, EDF has promised to continue to operate from Utilita’s headquarters near Southampton which is the base for about 600of Utilita’s employees.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva kicked off Thursday's agenda after China's President Xi Jinping's welcome note. Georgieva said that artificial intelligence and energy supply shocks had accelerated global inflation in many economies, calling for monetary policy tightening. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was met with another cold reception . She spent several minutes trying to talk to Xi who did not appear to respond with no interpreter present. Trump held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and Xi earlier in the day.

items.summary: The vehicles currently operate in 15 US cities, though freeway rides are only offered in a handful, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
items.body: Waymo has temporarily suspended driverless rides on US freeways after California banned the service over safety concerns. California's Department of Motor Vehicles said a series of traffic incidents, including robotaxis entering active construction zones, posed an imminent risk to public safety. Waymo has now restricted freeway operations in all other US markets while it reviews the performance of its vehicles. Waymo currently operates in 15 US cities, though only offered driverless freeway rides in a handful of cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.

items.title: Weight-loss drugs used in nearly one in 10 homes in Great Britain, study finds
items.summary: About 2.6m adults are taking the drugs, fuelled by the regulator’s approval of the pill versions and a rise in male users At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users…
items.body: At least one person is taking weight-loss drugs in 8.5% of households in Great Britain, according to research, meaning there are more homes with GLP-1 users than those containing vegetarians and pescatarians combined. About 2.6 million adults were using weight-loss medication in August, a rise of about 700,000 people since February, according to a survey by Worldpanel by Numerator . In February 6.3% of households had someone using GLP-1 drugs, rising to 8.5% in August. Weight-loss pills such as Wegovy were approved in the UK in June. Patients previously had to use the injectable version. Pills now account for more than one in 10 (11.2%) of GLP-1 users, while men are also driving the increase. Men make up just under a third (32%) of people taking weight-loss medication, up from 23% in February. Male users have nearly doubled to 830,000, up from 440,000 nine months ago.

items.title: Gold's bad year is getting worse. Why its price keeps falling
items.summary: Gold has fallen sharply from its January record as higher interest rates and a stronger dollar change the investment case for the precious metal.
items.body: Precious metals investors can be forgiven if they feel like the past year has given them whiplash. Following a torrid run, which saw the price of gold hit new records 53 times in 2025, gold hit a historic high of $5,589.38 an ounce on Jan. 28, only to take an almost equally historic nosedive. On Wednesday, gold fell below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025, roughly a third below its peak. A convergence of factors pushed gold to historic highs earlier this year, according to Suki Cooper, global head of commodities research at Standard Chartered, the London-based multinational bank. Now a different convergence is bringing the price down. Which role it plays depends on the factors dominating the market and the psyche of investors, and right now, it's the currency argument that is bringing the precious metal down.

items.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
items.summary: The company behind the Claude chatbot will become one of the most valuable firms in the world.
items.body: Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world. A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range. Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion. The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares. Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

items.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
items.summary: Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask Business live – latest updates Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as…
items.body: R oll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company . From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees . And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia .

items.title: Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019
items.summary: Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her trip to attend the APEC summit, as Beijing shows limited appetite for repairing ties strained by Taiwan dispute.
items.body: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her first trip to China as premier, signaling Beijing's limited appetite for repairing ties strained by a simmering row over Taiwan. At gatherings such as this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, protocol details — including who greets a visiting leader at the airport and where they are positioned in official photographs — often convey political messages. Takaichi was met on the tarmac Wednesday by a retired Chinese diplomat, rather than a serving official, and Japan's ambassador to China, Kenji Kanasugi. The low-key reception contrasted sharply with the warmer welcomes given to other visiting leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, while U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted personally by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

items.title: More support for households reliant on heating oil
items.summary: North Northamptonshire Council is encouraging eligible residents to apply for more support.
items.body: Households using heating oil as their main energy source are being offered more financial support by North Northamptonshire Council. Residents can apply for a £250 voucher in emergency situations where low oil levels would put health, safety or basic living conditions at risk. Heating oil is not protected by the Ofgem energy price cap, which means those reliant on it feel price increases faster than those on mains gas or electricity. The Reform UK-led council encouraged residents to see if they were eligible for support online , external . Heating oil prices have been volatile since the conflict between the US and Iran began in March. Rural areas, including parts of North Northamptonshire, are among the most affected, the council said.

items.title: In an authoritarian economy, Jensen Huang may be too big to fail | Robert Reich
items.summary: A handful of men control the US economy. They have leveraged themselves to be – or seem – indispensable Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners…
items.body: Jensen Huang has said he would return to Nvidia as its CEO if its board requests it. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said . “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang, who admitted being unfaithful to his wife, resigned from Nvidia last week. US intelligence agencies have identified one of his alleged lovers as a spy for China. If true, Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips may have found their way there. Beyond the tabloid headlines lies a much bigger story – a US economy that’s become dependent on the initiatives and decisions of a few powerful men who are too big to fail.

items.title: Data center electricity use could double by 2030, IEA says
items.summary: Global electricity use by data centers could double by 2030 as the AI boom adds pressure to power grids across the world, according to the IEA.
items.body: Global electricity use by data centers could double by 2030 and stretch power grids, potentially delaying new projects, the International Energy Agency warned. Data centers could consume around 1,000 terawatt-hours of electricity a year by 2030, according to the IEA, which added that tight supply chains, local opposition and limited grid capacity could slow construction. The warning is part of the IEA's Stated Policies Scenario , in which the agency forecasts are based on measures that have been put forward but have not yet been adopted. The IEA cites large data center project pipelines in Texas, Virginia, Finland and the U.K. In several regions, the combined capacity of data centers waiting to connect exceeds current peak demand. Without grid upgrades, power networks could become more congested and less reliable, the IEA said.

items.title: Increase in direct cremations since pandemic
items.summary: A 2026 Cost of Dying Report found direct cremation was now chosen for about one in five funerals.
items.body: Funeral directors say there has been an increase in direct cremations, with no mourners in attendance, since the Covid-19 pandemic. Brian Ugalde, whose firm of funeral directors has worked in Cornwall for 135 years, said non-attendance had become more acceptable since the lockdowns when families were not always allowed to attend. "A funeral is a ceremony... a farewell, a celebration... it is for for those left behind," he said, adding direct cremation came after Covid when "the model became acceptable and practical" as well as being cheaper. SunLife's 2026 Cost of Dying Report found direct cremation was now chosen for about one in five funerals in the UK. The report said, in the majority of cases, the deceased had requested or arranged a direct cremation themselves before their death.

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary: We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a…
items.body: O ver the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on.

items.title: Novartis raises blockbuster drug forecasts to $18 billion as it seeks to prove growth can last
items.summary: The drugmaker cited strong demand for its blockbuster drugs as it upgraded peak sales forecasts for multiple sclerosis, leukemia, and cholesterol medicines.
items.body: Pharma major Novartis is becoming more optimistic about some of its biggest growth drugs, even as investors question the company's ability to sustain growth beyond 2031 and offset the financial impact of older drugs' patent expiries. The Swiss drugmaker now expects multiple sclerosis drug Kesimpta, leukaemia treatment Scemblix, and cholesterol medicine Leqvio to generate $18 billion in peak sales, up from a previous forecast of $14 billion combined. CEO Vas Narasimhan said the upgrades were driven primarily by strong commercial performance, pointing to growing market share for Kesimpta and Scemblix and robust demand for Leqvio in the U.S. and Asia. "It's really that in-market commercial performance that's driving these upgrades," Narasimhan told reporters on Thursday. Shares fell 2.4% in mid-morning trading in Switzerland.

items.title: Leftover pumpkins help deliver 1,000th free meal
items.summary: "It's a really tough time for a lot of people," a sustainable food organisation says.
items.body: Leftover pumpkins have helped a sustainable food organisation provide its 1,000th free meal to low-income households. Cambridge Sustainable Food started producing recipe kits earlier this year using fruit and vegetables that would have otherwise gone to waste. The group received masses of pumpkins from local farmers after Halloween, including about 300kg (661lb) of them from one supplier alone. Alex Vardill, from the organisation, said many of the meal kits had been received by families who sometimes struggled to access fresh produce. "This has been a real help with improving that access at a time when food is really expensive," the 25-year-old said. "They provide everything you need to make a meal in one bag, already measured out, with a recipe there in front of you." The kits are funded by Cambridge City Council and South Cambridgeshire District Council.

items.title: Leaseholders in England and Wales to have ground rent capped in 2028
items.summary: Housing minister hails ‘historic moment’ as he publishes bill to eventually ban almost all new leasehold properties Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban…
items.body: Leaseholders in England and Wales will have their ground rent capped in 2028, the housing minister has said as he publishes a bill that will eventually ban virtually all new leasehold properties. Matthew Pennycook will introduce the government’s leasehold reform bill on Thursday, including measures to cap charges, end the sale of new leasehold flats and make it easier to extend and buy out leases. He said one of the first elements of the bill to come into force would be the long-promised £250 cap on annual ground rent – though it will not be enacted as quickly as some MPs have pushed for. “The ground rent can be expected fairly early,” he said. “I think it will be a really historic moment … leasehold denies individuals control over the homes they live in and have paid for.

items.title: Musk accuses Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield restrictions in Ukraine
items.summary: Elon Musk was asked about Zelenskyy claims over the Starshield network, and he said, "I don't want to blow your mind, but Zelenskyy is not always truthful."
items.body: SpaceX founder Elon Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being untruthful about restrictions around Ukraine's Starshield network and said Kyiv wanted to use Starlink for offensive operations. Asked at The New York Times' Dealbook Summit about Zelenskyy's claims that Starshield had been slowed down, Musk said, "That's false ... I don't want to blow your mind, but Zelenskyy is not always truthful." When pressed on whether he meant Ukraine was not always truthful, Musk doubled down with a reply: "No, it's not always truthful." His comments came after Zelenskyy on Wednesday said speed restrictions remained in place on Starshield, hampering Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missile and drone strikes. "We are discussing this with the American side," he said.

items.body: Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump ’s “Make America great again” movement since 2024. “I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia. “I’m not sure what Maga means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla added. Musk famously declared at a 2024 campaign rally in Madison Square Garden: “I’m not just Maga.

items.title: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
items.summary: An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO.
items.body: An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO . Jaan Tallinn co-founded Skype and later sold it to eBay . He led Anthropic's first funding round, a $124 million Series A, five years ago — well before the company's Claude chatbot was on the market and took Wall Street and Silicon Valley by storm. Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT in what could be the largest IPO of all time, and the first public debut for an AI lab. Tallinn's exact holdings haven't been disclosed. But given Anthropic's expected debut valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, the return on his initial investment could be well into the tens of billions. His exact return would depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares along the way.

items.title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages
items.summary: As Democrats flag AI bank breaches and cyber-attacks in Japan, Jay Clayton says system failures happen US politics live – latest updates A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix…
items.body: A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more. “The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” Cantwell and Rounds wrote to Clayton, who is also serving as the White House AI czar.

items.body: Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”. The prime minister also believes his proposed changes to welfare are a “very different proposition” from those of his predecessor, Keir Starmer, and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in the last government. On Tuesday, a report suggested national insurance contributions (NICs) paid by firms for under-25s should be gradually lowered, starting with retail and hospitality companies, to help create more jobs. The independent report , by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, also proposed doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. Asked if he believed the last government was wrong to increase NICs, Burnham told LBC: “I think it’s something you’ve got to consider very carefully going forward.

items.title: Nvidia’s Kress faces a divided workforce as some employees push for Huang’s return

items.body: The day before Colette Kress led her first earnings call as Nvidia's interim CEO, she did not want to talk about her predecessor, Jensen Huang . "This is a new era for Nvidia," she told employees in an internal meeting on Monday, according to a person present, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. When someone brought up Huang, Kress quickly changed the subject, according to the person. On Wednesday, Kress addressed the whole company at the first Nvidia all-hands meeting since the public chaos over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and other reported relationships. And while Kress will be tasked with filling the leadership vacuum created by Huang's departure, she is also tamping down public calls to bring him back. Huang himself weighed in with his first public statement Tuesday saying he would be "honored" to return to Nvidia.

items.body: Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning , about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours bike courier to support his young family, with Boyle in mind. Clio Barnard was on board to direct. After meeting Walsh at the stage door, Boyle went away and became one of the most charismatic and watchable actors of his generation.

items.title: 'Parasite' backer and other South Korean media, gaming and travel stocks rally on China trade deal
items.summary: Korean media, gaming and travel stocks surged on hopes of greater access to China.
items.body: South Korean entertainment, gaming and travel stocks surged Thursday as Seoul and Beijing largely concluded a trade deal, allowing Korean companies greater access to China's vast consumer market. South Korean entertainment industry has faced Chinese curbs for nearly a decade, and a deal stands to open up new revenue streams for Seoul's media, gaming and tourism industries. Drama producer Studio Dragon — who created the drama Crash Landing on You — soared 29.96%, while media giant CJ ENM, which backed the Oscar-winning film "Parasite," jumped 26% early Thursday. Travel agency Hana Tour rose 18%, while film distributor Showbox gained 9%. South Korea's gaming stocks Krafton and Shift Up advanced 2.69% and 6.57%, respectively.

items.title: Alibaba trains next-gen AI model on own chips amid tighter US curbs
items.body: HONG KONG -- Facing tightened access to advanced U.S. artificial intelligence chips, Alibaba Group is already training its next-generation AI model on proprietary chips from T-Head, the company's chip unit that recently was approved for an IPO in Hong Kong, CEO Eddie Wu said on Thursday.

items.title: One of the world's most contested seas is proving too much for Asia's leaders to resolve
items.summary: The ASEAN summit in the Philippines failed to conclude the Code of Conduct for the South China Sea despite Manila pledging it would happen this year.
items.body: One of the world's most contested bodies of water continues to cause problems for Asia's leaders. A substantive Code of Conduct in the South China Sea does not seem to be feasible despite ASEAN nations expressing optimism that the negotiations could finally conclude after more than two decades, experts told CNBC. The ASEAN summit in the Philippines failed to resolve it, despite Manila saying it intended to conclude the Code this year. The crux of the issue is that China claims virtually all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite international rulings saying it's not the case and historical claims from many other countries. China's "nine-dash line" claim was ruled as invalid by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, although Beijing has refused to recognize that ruling.

items.title: Xi, Trump, Putin promise to raise energy supplies and lower nuclear risk
items.body: SHENZHEN -- China, the U.S. and Russia plan to increase the production and supply of refined oil and said they will engage in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks and prevent proliferation, according to a joint statement released after a historic meeting of their presidents on Thursday.
